types.orientation: Introductory account useful to a Nihaya reader.
types.foundation: A philosophical basis needed to interpret a logical distinction.
types.qualification: A substantive difference or restriction that should not be flattened.
types.logical-tool: A specific logical distinction used by the philosophical argument.

policy.negativeRule: Lexical occurrence never generates a curated cross-text link.
policy.review: Passages are read and an exact quoted anchor is recorded. This is editorial analysis, not independent specialist certification.
policy.bidirectional: Each curated route has an explicit reverse route when its paired reading is useful; the builder does not manufacture semantic inverses.

terms.definition: Cognition involving affirmation or negation. Muẓaffar describes apprehension of a relation’s accord with reality as entailing judgment; Ṭabāṭabāʾī analyses judgment as an act of the soul. The related formulations should be compared without assuming that assent, conception of a relation, and judgment are identical.

discussions.note: The soul’s synthesis of concepts in judgment

terms.label: Self-evident and discursive knowledge
terms.definition: Self-evident cognition requires no further learning or inferential inquiry; theoretical or discursive cognition does. This distinction applies to conception and assent. It differs from the division between representational knowledge (ḥuṣūlī) and knowledge by presence.

discussions.note: Immediate and discursive conception and assent

discussions.note: Why discursive cognition depends on immediate cognition

discussions.note: The chain of proof must terminate in premises not acquired by further proof.

discussions.quote: The self-evident propositions most worthy of acceptance are the primary propositions.
discussions.note: The special role of primary propositions.

terms.label: Natural universal
terms.definition: The nature considered without adding universality as a logical attribute. Its occurrence in individuals is distinct from the mind’s consideration of that nature as predicable of many.

terms.definition: A universal can be predicated of many even by supposition. Particularity excludes such sharing. The texts distinguish this from the individuation of a cognitive state in one knower.

Under the aspect mentioned—that is, its subsisting in and qualifying a particular soul, and likewise its being one of the soul’s qualities and a perfection of it—the intelligible quiddity is one of the external existents that fall outside our discussion. We are discussing quiddity with its mental existence, in which
discussions.note: A concept’s mental universality distinguished from its being an individual cognitive state.

discussions.note: Adding universal descriptions does not yield individual existence.

terms.definition: Predication through identity of concept or quiddity, with a difference in consideration. Contrast common predication through unity of concrete instance.

terms.definition: Predication based on unity of instance despite difference of concept. Merely conceiving a substance or quality does not make the mind an external instance of it.

terms.label: Privation and possession
terms.definition: An opposed absence and positive condition in a subject naturally capable of that condition; distinct from unrestricted negation.

terms.label: Graded predication
terms.definition: Variation in the way a universal predicate applies to its instances, as in intensity or priority. This logical classification must be distinguished from the metaphysical thesis that the very reality of existence is one and graded.

terms.label: Gradation of existence
terms.definition: The thesis that existence is one reality whose degrees differ in the very respect in which they agree. It is stronger than merely classifying a universal predicate as graded.

discussions.note: Existential divisions distinguished from quiddative multiplicity.

discussions.quote: The one and the many are thus each an instance of the one.
discussions.note: The difference between one and many returns to their common existential ground.

terms.label: Special possibility
terms.definition: Absence of intrinsic necessity on both sides, affirmation and negation. In an existential context it is the contingency of a quiddity considered in itself.

discussions.note: Neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary for the quiddity.

discussions.note: Special possibility distinguished from ordinary general possibility.

discussions.quote: The answer is that qualification by an attribute among concrete things does not require that attribute to be realized among them through a separate, independent existence.
discussions.note: Its status as a philosophical intelligible grounded through the subject.

terms.label: General possibility
terms.definition: Absence of necessity on the opposite side, without deciding whether the affirmed side is itself necessary. This is broader than special possibility.

discussions.note: General possibility in affirmative and negative predications.

discussions.quote: “Human is necessarily an animal” has necessity both as its real matter and as its expressed qualification.
discussions.note: Expressing a necessary relation with the weaker qualifier possible.

terms.label: Ground of assent
terms.definition: That through which a judgment is justified, distinguished from the cause that makes the fact obtain. A logical reason and an existential cause need not be identical.

terms.label: Cause of being
terms.definition: That which explains the thing’s existence or the fact’s obtaining, as distinct from what explains someone’s assent to it.

terms.label: Intellectual consideration
terms.definition: A family of uses of iʿtibārī, not one undifferentiated doctrine. Logical concepts such as genus and universal qualify mental instances; philosophical concepts such as possibility are predicated in thought while their subjects are qualified externally. Elsewhere the term can concern quiddity’s derivative status, dependent relation, or practical convention. None of these senses alone means arbitrary fiction.

discussions.note: Possibility considered with quiddity.

discussions.note: Philosophical possibility has mental predication and external qualification.

terms.definition: An argument composed of propositions such that accepting them entails another proposition by virtue of their composition. In this logical sense qiyās is distinct from juristic analogy.

terms.definition: A syllogism in which neither the conclusion nor its contradictory is expressly given as a whole in the premises. Its premises may be categorical or conditional.

terms.label: Existence
terms.definition: The primary concept by which something is understood as existing. Its univocal conceptual meaning is distinguished from the concrete reality and degrees of existence; a definition clearer than this primary concept is unavailable.

discussions.quote: Both conception and assent are divided into two kinds.
discussions.note: Being is an example of an immediate conception.

discussions.quote: Existence, as a concept, is shared in meaning: it is predicated with one meaning of everything of which it is predicated.
discussions.note: The single meaning predicated of different existents.

terms.label: Quiddity
terms.definition: What is given in answer to What is it? Considered in its defining content, it includes neither existence nor nonexistence, although its actual instance is never exempt from both.

discussions.quote: Once you have conceived the word's meaning in a general way, you turn naturally to the second stage: seeking a conception of the meaning's quiddity.

discussions.quote: Quiddity (māhiyya), which is “what is said in answer to the question ‘What is it?’,” does not, considered as such and with regard to its own essence, preclude being characterized as existent or nonexistent.

terms.label: Concept / instance
terms.definition: A concept is the meaning considered in thought; an instance is what that meaning applies to in the relevant consideration. The mental existence of a concept does not establish external existence, real possibility, or numerical identity of its represented object.

discussions.note: Particular and universal concepts, including nonexistence.

discussions.quote: The answer is that nothing can be asserted of the absolutely nonexistent insofar as it is sheer nullity in reality.

terms.definition: In the five-predicable discussion, a predicate belonging to the subject’s constitutive quiddity. This sense of essential must be distinguished from other technical uses in demonstration, modality, and divine attributes.

discussions.quote: **1. Essential predicate.** This belongs to the constitution of a subject's essence and is not extrinsic to it: the subject's quiddity cannot be constituted without it. The essential predicate may be the whole quiddity, as *human being* is predicated of Zayd or ʿAmr, or an essential part, as *animal* and *rational* are predicated of
discussions.note: Species, genus, and differentia as constitutive predicables.

discussions.quote: The intelligible meanings included in a quiddity's definition, such that removal of any one would remove that quiddity, are called its *essential constituents* (dhātiyyāt).
discussions.note: Inclusion in the defining account.

discussions.quote: An essential predicate is distinguished from what is not essential by its properties, which are consequences of its being essential.
discussions.note: Necessity and explanatory properties of essential predication.

terms.label: Accidental predicate
terms.definition: A predicate outside a subject’s constitutive definition, whether separable or necessary. It is not synonymous with an ontological accident inhering in a subject, and accidental does not simply mean temporary.

discussions.quote: A second ambiguity arises because logicians call an extrinsic universal a special or common *ʿaraḍ*, and then also call such a thing as laughter an *ʿaraḍ*.
discussions.note: The explicit distinction between accidental predication and inhering accident.

discussions.quote: Accidental predicates are further distinguished.
discussions.note: Predicates requiring an added attribute and predicates abstracted without one.

discussions.quote: An accidental predicate is of two kinds. If its abstraction and predication depend upon the conjunction of something with the subject, as the abstraction of “hot” and its predication of a body depend upon the conjunction of heat with that body, it is called “a predicate through an added attribute” (maḥmūl bi-l-ḍamīma). If they do not
discussions.note: The developed distinction between the two kinds.

terms.label: Genus
terms.definition: The shared essential constituent of different species, considered so that it can be predicated of them. Its position in an ordered classification differs from the matter/form analysis made under a different consideration.

discussions.quote: **2. Near and remote genus.** Universals can form an ordered series under one another, such as human being → animal → growing body → body → substance. Moving upward from human being, the next term, animal, is the **proximate genus**, also called the lowest genus in the series. Above it lie successively more general genera, until the
discussions.note: Proximate, remote, and highest genera.

discussions.quote: Some essential meanings occur in several species, while others are particular to one.
discussions.note: The common essential constituent.

discussions.quote: It has been explained in logic that some of the essential meanings of species included in their definitions are shared by more than one species, such as animal, which is shared by human being, horse, and others.
discussions.note: The logical classification explicitly used in metaphysics.

terms.label: Differentia
terms.definition: The specific essential determinant within a genus. A logical differentia used in a definition may be a familiar concomitant standing in place of the difficult-to-know real constituent; the two should not be silently identified.

discussions.quote: Yet scholars acknowledge that grasping things' true essences and differentiæ is extraordinarily difficult and may be unattainable.
discussions.note: Why real differentiae are difficult to discover.

discussions.quote: The logical differentia is the most distinctive and best-known concomitant belonging to a species.
discussions.note: The logical substitute for the real differentia.

discussions.quote: The first is the most specific and best known of the concomitants that accrue to a species.
discussions.note: The example of rationality and the distinction of senses.

terms.label: Species
terms.definition: A complete quiddity with its own proper effects. A real species is distinguished from a relative species, which can be a species with respect to a higher genus while remaining a genus of lower kinds.

discussions.quote: “What is he?”, however, asks about the reality through which this individual shares an essence with others.
discussions.note: The what-is-it answer as species.

discussions.quote: A complete quiddity which, in virtue of its completeness, has its own proper real effects is called a *species* (nawʿ), as with the human being or the horse.
discussions.note: The complete quiddity with proper effects.

discussions.quote: It is divided into that whose effects follow from it upon nothing further than the external existence that individuates it as an individual, such as the human being.
discussions.note: Real and relative species.

terms.label: Substance / accident
terms.definition: Quiddities distinguished by whether their external existence is in a subject independent of them. An accidental predicate in logic is a different classification: a predicate outside a definition need not itself be an inhering accident.

discussions.quote: A second ambiguity arises because logicians call an extrinsic universal a special or common *ʿaraḍ*, and then also call such a thing as laughter an *ʿaraḍ*.
discussions.note: The two technical senses of accident.

discussions.quote: Quiddity is divided at the outset into *substance* and *accident*.
discussions.note: Substance defined through its mode of existence.

discussions.quote: Quiddity divides primarily into a quiddity which, when it exists externally, exists not in a subject independent of it—this is the quiddity of substance—and a quiddity which, when it exists externally, exists in a subject independent of it—these are the nine accidental categories.
discussions.note: The primary quiddative division.

terms.label: Complete essential definition
terms.definition: An account expressing all constitutive essentials through the proximate genus and differentia. A clear description can distinguish an object without demonstrating knowledge of its real differentia.

discussions.quote: A complete essential definition states all the essential constituents of what is being defined.
discussions.note: The complete logical definition.

discussions.quote: Some essential meanings occur in several species, while others are particular to one.
discussions.note: Genus and differentia as the essential constituents.

discussions.quote: Substance, then, is a quiddity which, when it exists externally, exists not in a subject independent of it.
discussions.note: Why a highest genus cannot have this kind of definition.

terms.label: Explanation of the name
terms.definition: An account making the intended meaning explicit, without by itself establishing the object’s existence or supplying a real essential definition. Compare the logical sequence of questions with philosophical explanations of primary concepts.

discussions.quote: The interrogative mā here is called explanatory (shāriḥa), because it asks for an explanation of what a word signifies.
discussions.note: Nominal accounts before an existence judgment.

discussions.quote: Accordingly, expressions offered as definitions—such as saying that existence, or an existent as existent, is “that which is established in reality,” or “that about which a statement can be made”—are explanations of a name, not genuine definitions.
discussions.note: Attempted definitions of existence as explanations.

discussions.quote: These are all verbal definitions, explanations of a name that serve to draw attention to its meaning, rather than real definitions.
discussions.note: Why modal notions receive explanations rather than real definitions.

terms.label: Circularity
terms.definition: In definition, explaining a thing through something whose own explanation already requires the first thing. This dependence in knowing is distinct from a circle in the existence of efficient causes.

discussions.quote: Fourth, the account must not be circular. Circularity arises when the expression offered to explain the subject is itself unintelligible except through that subject. The subject then becomes part of its own explanation.
discussions.note: The logical prohibition of circular definition.

discussions.quote: Unity and multiplicity are among the most general concepts impressed upon the mind immediately, like existence and possibility.
discussions.note: Application to proposed definitions of unity and multiplicity.

discussions.quote: An existent is divided into the one and the many: every existent is either one or many.
discussions.note: The expanded diagnosis of the same circularity.

terms.label: Causal circularity
terms.definition: The existence of a thing depending, directly or through intermediaries, upon something whose existence depends on it. The objection concerns existential priority, not merely a circular wording of definitions.

discussions.quote: A causal circle (*dawr*) is impossible. It occurs when the existence of something depends on what itself depends upon that thing, whether directly, an *explicit circle*, or through one or more intermediaries, a *concealed circle*. In either case the thing's existence ultimately depends upon itself. Since a cause is prior to its effect in
discussions.note: Explicit and concealed causal circles.

discussions.quote: Circularity is a thing’s existence depending upon something whose existence depends upon it.
discussions.note: Direct and mediated existential dependence.

terms.label: Contradiction
terms.definition: Affirmation and negation of exactly the same content under the required common respects. The two cannot both obtain and cannot both fail to obtain. Primary and common predication must not be mixed when diagnosing a contradiction.

discussions.quote: **Notice.** These eight unities are those commonly recognized among logicians.
discussions.note: Unity of predication in addition to the ordinary unities.

discussions.quote: Contradictories neither coexist nor are both absent.
discussions.note: The first principle of judgment.

discussions.quote: Two contradictories cannot both be true and cannot both be false.
discussions.note: Contradiction as genuine disjunction.

terms.label: Contrariety
terms.definition: Opposition between positive determinations that cannot coexist in the same subject, time, and respect. The developed Peripatetic account adds a proximate genus and maximal difference. It differs from contradiction and from the special opposition between quantified propositions.

discussions.quote: **3. Contrary opposition (taqābul al-ḍiddayn)**: hot/cold, black/white, virtue/vice, rashness/cowardice, lightness/heaviness. Contraries are two positive attributes successively capable of belonging to one subject but incapable of existing together in that same subject. Conceiving one does not require conceiving the other. The phrase
discussions.note: The logical introduction to contrary attributes.

discussions.quote: Rather, according to the traditional inductive analysis, contrariety is between ultimate species falling under a proximate genus, as black and white under colour.
discussions.note: Contraries under a proximate genus.

discussions.quote: The Peripatetics, however, added further qualifications to what follows from the division.
discussions.note: The further Peripatetic qualifications.

terms.label: Correlation
terms.definition: Reciprocal relational descriptions whose conceptions require one another, such as father and child. Their simultaneity as correlatives does not erase the existential priority of a cause over its effect.

discussions.quote: **4. Correlative opposition (taqābul al-mutaḍāyifayn)**: father/son, above/below, earlier/later, cause/effect, creator/creature. Three points explain their distinctive structure. First, conceiving either requires conceiving its correlate: to understand something as a father or cause is to understand it as having a son or effect. Second,
discussions.note: Reciprocal concepts and the same-respect restriction.

discussions.quote: It follows that the two correlatives, considered precisely as correlatives, are simultaneous: neither precedes the other in the mind or outside it.
discussions.note: The co-presence of correlated descriptions.

discussions.quote: As the division has shown, two correlatives are two existent features, one of which cannot be conceived without conceiving the other.
discussions.note: The philosophical account of correlative opposition.

terms.label: Relation
terms.definition: As a category, a configuration grounded in reciprocal reference. It must be distinguished from a pure existential connection constituted in its terms, and from the mere logical relation of concepts.

discussions.quote: **4. Correlative opposition (taqābul al-mutaḍāyifayn)**: father/son, above/below, earlier/later, cause/effect, creator/creature. Three points explain their distinctive structure. First, conceiving either requires conceiving its correlate: to understand something as a father or cause is to understand it as having a son or effect. Second,
discussions.note: Correlative concepts as the logical comparison.

discussions.quote: **Relation** (iḍāfa) is the determination arising from a reciprocal reference between two things.
discussions.note: A categorial relation and its reciprocal terms.

discussions.quote: You have learned that seven of the categories are relational accidents: relation, where, when, position, possession, acting, and being acted upon.
discussions.note: Why a relational category is not the bare connective existence.

terms.label: Linking existence
terms.definition: A mode of being constituted in its terms rather than independently subsisting alongside them. Particle-like meaning illustrates the nonindependence, while the metaphysical arguments concern real connections and an effect’s dependence upon its cause.

discussions.quote: **3. Particle (adāh).** Corresponding to the grammarians' *ḥarf*, this signifies a relation between two terms: *fī* (“in”) expresses containment, *ʿalā* (“upon”) elevation or superposition, and *hal* introduces interrogation. A relation is not independently intelligible in the same way as a substance or free-standing meaning because it
discussions.note: A linguistic illustration of dependent meaning.

discussions.quote: The being of the connection is constituted in its terms.
discussions.note: Connection distinguished from independent predicative existence.

discussions.quote: Is the difference between independent and connective existence a difference in kind, or is it not?
discussions.note: Why an effect can be connective relative to its cause and independently conceived in another consideration.

terms.label: Existence for another
terms.definition: An existence that actualises its own quiddity while, by that same existence, removes a privation from another, as knowledge removes ignorance from its subject. It differs from a pure connection without independent conceptual content.

discussions.quote: For example, knowledge actualises its own quiddity as a quality and, by that very existence, removes ignorance from the soul in which it occurs.
discussions.note: Knowledge and power as examples.

discussions.quote: By a thing’s existence being for another, we mean that its existence in itself—the existence that excludes nonexistence from its quiddity—is itself also what excludes nonexistence from something else.
discussions.note: The developed account of one existence perfecting its subject.

terms.label: The fact of the matter
terms.definition: What obtains in the relevant order to which a true proposition conforms. It is not restricted to currently external individuals: mental classifications and truths involving nonexistence require appropriate accounts of establishment.

discussions.quote: **1. Assertion (khabar).** Sometimes the relation possesses a determinate reality independently of the words: the expression describes or discloses that reality. For example, if rain has fallen or is expected tomorrow, one may say “It rained” or “It will rain tomorrow.” This is an assertion, also called a proposition (*qaḍiyya*) or
discussions.note: Truth as correspondence of assertion.

discussions.quote: The broad kind of establishment embracing existence, quiddity, and these intellectual concepts is called *nafs al-amr*—‘the fact of the matter’ or what actually obtains in the relevant order.
discussions.note: The general domain of true predication.

discussions.quote: The domain that the intellect supposes for establishment and realization without qualification in this last sense is what we call “the order of things themselves.” It encompasses true mental and external propositions and what the intellect affirms without a corresponding object mentally or externally.
discussions.note: The expanded account embracing external, mental, and further judgments.

terms.label: Necessity / possibility or contingency / impossibility
terms.definition: The three real modal alternatives: necessary affirmation, necessary negation, or neither necessity. Logic applies the distinction to subject–predicate relations generally; philosophy here applies it to existence and its essential attributes.

discussions.quote: **3. The matter (mādda) of a proposition.** For every predicate attributed to a subject, the predicative relation, considered as it actually obtains in reality (*nafs al-amr*), falls under exactly one of three modes by rational division.
discussions.note: The matter of any predicative relation.

discussions.quote: Whenever a concept is considered in relation to existence, one of three alternatives must hold.
discussions.note: The division relative to existence.

discussions.quote: The three modalities mentioned are not restricted to propositions whose predicate is existence.
discussions.note: The explicit distinction between logical and philosophical scope.

terms.label: Relative necessity
terms.definition: Necessity disclosed when something is compared with another, including the concomitance of a complete cause and effect. It differs from necessity bestowed through a cause and from an agent’s merely incomplete causal role.

discussions.quote: In a necessary connection, a genuine relation entails that one side follows from the other.
discussions.note: Logical concomitance can have several causal directions.

discussions.quote: **Necessity in itself** is exemplified by the Necessary Existent, exalted is He: His very reality suffices for the necessity of His existence without need of anything besides Himself.
discussions.note: Comparative necessity distinguished from necessity through another.

discussions.quote: This is necessity relative to another, distinct from the necessity through another discussed earlier in the proposition, “A thing does not exist unless it becomes necessary.”
discussions.note: The explicit distinction in complete causality.

terms.label: Complete cause
terms.definition: Everything upon which the effect’s occurrence depends, such that no further requisite remains. Its presence entails the effect; identifying such completeness is a separate epistemic task and is not guaranteed by observing a resemblance or regular succession.

discussions.quote: We may, however, know that the common feature—the respect of resemblance—is a **complete cause** of the judgment’s presence in the original case.
discussions.note: The condition for a certain inference beyond analogy.

discussions.quote: A cause may be **complete** or **incomplete**.
discussions.note: Complete versus incomplete cause.

discussions.quote: Cause is divided into complete and incomplete.
discussions.note: The expanded definition.

terms.label: Cause / effect
terms.definition: An existent on which another depends, and the dependent existent. Distinguish the cause of being from a ground of assent, and distinguish existential dependence from the reciprocal concepts cause and effect.

discussions.quote: If a respondent has answered either the simple or composite hal, you proceed to the fifth stage: seeking the cause.
discussions.note: Ground of a judgment versus cause of the fact.

discussions.quote: This dependence must be upon an *existent* other, since the non-existent as non-existent has no thingness.
discussions.note: Existential dependence.

discussions.quote: It was established earlier that quiddity, considered in itself, is neither existent nor nonexistent.
discussions.note: The philosophical establishment of causality.

terms.label: Demonstration
terms.definition: Inference intended to yield certain knowledge through appropriately warranted premises. Formal syllogistic validity alone does not certify certainty or truth of the premises. The available Muẓaffar units introduce the five arts but do not include the later full Book of Demonstration.

discussions.quote: **First, in respect of its matter:** the differences between its premises are considered apart from their form.
discussions.note: Demonstration classified by the matter of a syllogism.

discussions.quote: Discursive sciences ultimately depend upon immediate cognitions by which their conclusions are established.
discussions.note: Discursive sciences grounded in immediate cognition.

discussions.quote: In other words, it must be an investigation in which we restrict ourselves to demonstration.
discussions.note: The demonstrative requirement of philosophical inquiry.

terms.label: Demonstration through the cause
terms.definition: A demonstration in which the explanatory cause supplies the ground of knowing why the conclusion holds, not merely a reason for accepting that it holds. Compare its limits where the subject has no external cause.

discussions.quote: If a respondent has answered either the simple or composite hal, you proceed to the fifth stage: seeking the cause.
discussions.note: Seeking both a ground of assent and the cause of the fact.

discussions.quote: Here *universal knowledge* is a form that does not change when the externally known object changes.
discussions.note: Causal knowledge remaining invariant through an event’s changes.

discussions.quote: By cause here we mean the cause that necessitates the effect through the specific character of its causality, whether it is a cause through its quiddity, as four is the cause of evenness, or a cause through its external existence.
discussions.note: The demanding account of knowing a caused thing through its cause.

terms.label: Demonstration through an effect or sign
terms.definition: A that-demonstration or sign-based route distinguished from a why-demonstration. Nihāya restricts certain philosophical inference to general concomitances and expressly contests unrestricted inference from an effect to its cause; the English label must not collapse those distinctions.
replaces: Demonstration through an effect or sign

discussions.quote: If a respondent has answered either the simple or composite hal, you proceed to the fifth stage: seeking the cause.
discussions.note: The reason for assent can be sought without the cause of being.

discussions.quote: As for demonstration of the fact, it has been established in the Book of Demonstration in logic that proceeding from an effect to its cause does not yield certainty.
discussions.note: Why philosophical inquiry uses general concomitances.

discussions.quote: It is therefore clear from the foregoing that investigating a conclusion sought yields knowledge of it only by proceeding to it through its cause, if it has a cause, or through general concomitances, if it has no cause.
discussions.note: The restriction on effect-to-cause inference.

terms.label: Individuation
terms.definition: The character by which a thing cannot be shared by many. The metaphysical account locates this in existence, distinguishing it from relative differentiation by further universal descriptions.

discussions.quote: A human being apprehends concepts of the individual things he perceives: Muḥammad, this book, this pen, this rose, Baghdad, Najaf, and so forth.
discussions.note: The logical particular as not applicable to another.

discussions.quote: Two consequences follow. First, distinction is a relative description of a quiddity, whereas individuation concerns the thing itself and is not intrinsically a comparative relation. Second, distinction is compatible with universality: adding one universal concept to another still does not produce particularity, no matter how often the
discussions.note: Distinction and individuation contrasted.

discussions.quote: “What individuates a thing—in the sense of that through which it becomes incapable of being shared—is in reality nothing other than that thing’s existence itself, as the Second Teacher held.
discussions.note: Why adding universal features does not produce individuality.

terms.label: Signification
terms.definition: Awareness of one thing leading the mind to another through a recognised connection. The books compare conventional words with real causal signification when analysing speech, without identifying a causal sign with literal utterance.

discussions.quote: The knocking is the **sign** (*dāll*), the presence of the person is the **signified** (*madlūl*), and the sign's having this property is **signification** (*dalāla*).
discussions.note: The sign, signified, and intellectual transition.

discussions.quote: But suppose there were a real existent that naturally signified another real existent, such as an effect making its cause known or a perfection in an effect revealing a fuller perfection in its cause.
discussions.note: Real signification used in the analysis of speech.

discussions.quote: “If there were a real existent signifying something through real rather than conventional signification—such as an effect signifying that which produces it, or an effect signifying through its existential perfection the perfection present in its cause in a higher and nobler manner—it would be more entitled to be
discussions.note: The causal analogy and its philosophical context.

terms.label: Conventional signification
terms.definition: Signification grounded in instituted or customary designation, requiring knowledge of the convention. Its ordinary verbal form is the starting point, not the unqualified endpoint, of the discussions of divine speech.

discussions.quote: The reason a word signifies a meaning is the established intellectual connection between expression and meaning.
discussions.note: The learned expression–meaning bond.

discussions.quote: These philosophers also offer an account of *speech*.
discussions.note: Speech in ordinary usage.

discussions.quote: “In our ordinary usage, speech is an expression that signifies, through conventional designation, what is inwardly intended.
discussions.note: The explicitly conventional account before the metaphysical analogy.

terms.label: Soul
terms.definition: A principle of cognition and bodily governance. The metaphysical account describes a substance immaterial in essence while related to matter in activity; the developmental logical introduction should not be mistaken for a complete proof of that doctrine.

discussions.quote: First, the newly born child's soul possesses an innate capacity but no acquired, actual knowledge.
discussions.note: Capacity for knowledge before acquired actual cognitions.

discussions.quote: **The soul** is a substance immaterial in essence while related to matter in its activity.
discussions.note: The immateriality argument announced through knowledge.

discussions.quote: But this is false in light of what has been established in psychology: souls originate with the origination of bodies, according to the prevalent view, or through the motion of the substances of bodies after the bodies have originated.
discussions.note: The discussion of the soul’s origination and rejection of actual innate knowledge.

terms.label: Potentiality / actuality
terms.definition: Preparedness or capacity in relation to a possible perfection, and the possession of that perfection. Logical judgments must keep these respects distinct; real dispositional possibility is also distinguished from the intellectual consideration of quiddative possibility.

discussions.quote: 5. **Potentiality and actuality.** The two propositions must agree in potentiality and actuality. There is no contradiction between “Muḥammad is dead,” meaning potentially, and “Muḥammad is not dead,” meaning actually.
discussions.note: Potential and actual predications do not automatically contradict.

discussions.quote: This possibility is an extramental condition rather than a mere intellectual consideration of quiddity.
discussions.note: Graded preparedness distinguished from quiddative possibility.

discussions.quote: The existence of a thing among concrete entities, such that the effects sought from it follow upon it, is called “actuality,” and one says that its existence is actual.
discussions.note: The initial definitions of potential and actual existence.

discussions.quote: Moreover, we find that this relation varies in proximity and remoteness, intensity and weakness.
discussions.note: The argument from degrees of preparedness, followed by the continuous account of potential and actual existence.

terms.label: Primacy of existence
terms.definition: The thesis that concrete actuality belongs primarily to existence while quiddity is intellectually derived from it. Conceptual distinction does not turn a single concrete thing into two independently actual entities.

discussions.quote: Here is one demonstration. Quiddity considered simply as quiddity is indifferent to existence and nonexistence. If its emergence from that indifference into actuality, with the consequent real effects, occurred by quiddity alone rather than through existence, quiddity would turn into what it was not, an impossibility. Existence therefore
discussions.note: Argument from the indifference of quiddity.

discussions.quote: Quiddity differs from existence, since what is peculiar to each differs from what is shared.
discussions.note: The single concrete reality and its primary and derived aspects.

terms.label: The Necessary Existent
terms.definition: What exists necessarily through itself rather than through another. Logical universality of the concept is compatible with the demonstrated impossibility of a second real instance; it does not mean that such a second instance is metaphysically possible.

discussions.quote: Conversely, a universal may have only one existent instance, with any second instance being impossible.
discussions.note: Conceptual universality does not dispense with a proof of unity.

discussions.quote: The Necessary Existent, exalted is He, is the pure reality of existence, which has no second.
discussions.note: True unity distinguished from numerical unity.

discussions.quote: It became clear in the preceding chapters that the essence of the intrinsically Necessary is existence itself, without a quiddity or any negative component.
discussions.note: The developed argument from pure existence.

terms.label: Univocal predication
terms.definition: One intelligible meaning predicated of several subjects, rather than a shared verbal sound concealing different meanings. Semantic univocity (ishtirāk maʿnawī) differs from uniform application (tawāṭuʾ): the same concept of existence can apply to graded instances.

discussions.quote: First, consider a universal such as human being, animal, gold or silver, and apply it to its individuals.
discussions.note: Comparison with uniform application: distinguish this classification from merely sharing one meaning.

discussions.quote: Existence is predicated of its subjects with one meaning: the term has a common intelligible signification, not merely the same verbal sound.
discussions.note: Existence has a single intelligible meaning.

discussions.quote: Existence, as a concept, is shared in meaning: it is predicated with one meaning of everything of which it is predicated.
discussions.note: The advanced account of semantic sharing.

terms.label: The predication of existence
terms.definition: The intellect’s attribution of existence to a quiddity distinguished in conception. It is not ordinary categorial inherence presupposing an already actual subject; simple existence judgments differ from predicating an additional attribute of an existent subject.

discussions.quote: Once these stages are completed, one naturally passes to the fourth stage, seeking assent that some attribute or condition belongs to the thing.
discussions.note: Simple and composite existential questions.

discussions.quote: The ‘accruing’ (ʿurūḍ) of existence to a quiddity, and its being established for that quiddity, is not an instance of categorial inherence in which an accident requires its subject to be already actual.
discussions.note: Why existence does not accrue as an ordinary accident.

discussions.quote: Sixth, existence supervenes upon quiddity. This means that the intellect can strip quiddity of existence and understand it by itself, without considering its existence. Existence is therefore neither identical with it nor part of it. Evidence for this includes the possibility of negating existence of quiddity, the need for proof that it
discussions.note: The intellectual distinction underlying the predication.

terms.label: Logical universal
terms.definition: Universality considered as the mental attribute of being applicable to many, distinct from the nature qualified and from the nature considered together with that qualification.

discussions.quote: **2. The logical universal (*al-kullī al-manṭiqī*).** The intellect considers the abstract characteristic of being a universal—“that which may be supposed to apply to many”—without attaching it to any particular nature, such as human, animal, or stone. It exists only in the intellect, for it is a purely mental concept formed by
discussions.note: The logical universal as distinguished from the natural universal.

discussions.quote: A *considered* or *intellectually abstracted* concept is not of this kind.
discussions.note: Logical concepts whose proper instances are mental.

discussions.quote: As for meanings whose instances are characterized precisely by being mental, our minds can take something abstracted from external reality—which is a concept—as an instance and consider it.
discussions.note: How the intellect abstracts logical classifications from concepts.

terms.label: Concept as a title
terms.definition: The use of a concept to direct a judgment toward what it represents. Compare the concept as an object of judgment with the immediate cognitive form and the external object known by attribution; these distinctions explain different respects of representation without identifying them all.

discussions.quote: One may instead look beyond the concept to what it represents.
discussions.note: The concept as title and its intended referent.

discussions.quote: First, what is known through acquired knowledge is divided into the **immediately known** (*maʿlūm bi-l-dhāt*) and the **known by attribution** (*maʿlūm bi-l-ʿaraḍ*).
discussions.note: Immediately known form versus external object known by attribution.

discussions.quote: First: a mental quiddity does not fall under, and is not included in, the category under which it fell when it was external and its effects followed upon it.
discussions.note: Why representing a category is not becoming an external instance of it.

terms.label: Good and evil
terms.definition: In these texts, good is existence or an existential perfection sought by a thing; evil considered in itself is the absence of a thing or of its perfection. Distinguish a harmful existent, called evil incidentally, from the privation it occasions. The fivefold classification admits pure good and predominant good. Nihāya additionally examines pain as knowledge by presence and the incidental place of evil in divine decree.

discussions.quote: In killing, for example, the evil is not the killer's power, which is a positive perfection in its own respect,
discussions.note: Privation and the sword-and-killing example in the reply to dualism.

discussions.quote: Another reply, attributed to Aristotle, divides possible things into five: what is pure good; what contains much good and little evil; what contains equal good and evil; what contains much evil and little good; and what is pure evil.
discussions.note: The fivefold classification and the existence of pure and predominant good.

discussions.quote: Good is what every thing seeks, intends, and loves, and toward which every thing naturally turns.
discussions.note: The definitions of good and evil through existential perfection and privation.

discussions.quote: If, for example, a man kills another with a sword after restraining him,
discussions.note: The developed sword example distinguishing positive capacities from loss of life.

discussions.quote: I reply: Ṣadr al-Mutaʾallihīn—may his secret be sanctified—answered that pain is the apprehension of an adverse privative condition, such as disruption of continuity and the like, through knowledge by presence.
discussions.note: The reply to the pain objection through knowledge by presence.

discussions.quote: For, as reported from the First Teacher, things fall into five divisions in respect of the goods and evils attributed to them: pure good, pure evil, predominance of good, predominance of evil, and equality of good and evil.
discussions.note: The five divisions, developed in the following paragraphs.

discussions.quote: It follows that evils enter into divine decree through a secondary intention.
discussions.note: Evil’s incidental inclusion in divine decree through a secondary intention.
